# External demonstrations of the validity ladder (run 24 Sep 2026)

Two releases generated by other groups, run through levels 2 and 3.

**Update 26 Sep 2026.** The level-2 verdicts in this file use the old script-66 rule and are superseded. The R3 verdicts are in `../../analysis/brm/l2_external_r3*.csv` (script 78e), reported in `../analysis_brm/L2.md` section 5. Level-3 results here still stand. Nothing was generated for this; every silicon answer below comes from the original authors' files.

| Release | What it holds | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Meister, Guestrin & Hashimoto 2024, "Benchmarking Distributional Alignment of LLMs" (arXiv 2411.05403) | Steered answer distributions on 100 contested OpinionQA questions (Pew ATP) from GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3 Opus and Llama-3-70B; three elicitation methods (verbalised distribution, 30-sample sequence, token log-probabilities); persona and few-shot steering; the Pew group targets | `raw/meister2024/` (git clone, commit 36869b5) |
| Argyle et al. 2023, "Out of One, Many", Political Analysis, Study 3 | 4,270 ANES 2016 respondents. For each of 12 interview questions GPT-3 davinci saw the respondent's own answers to the other 11 and answered the omitted one, so every silicon answer has a human twin. Main run at temperature 0.7, repeats at 0.001 and 1.0 | `raw/argyle2023/` (Harvard Dataverse doi:10.7910/DVN/JPV20K) |

Santurkar et al.'s own OpinionQA runs sit on CodaLab, which timed out all evening (direct and through a proxy). The Meister release uses the same questions and the same Pew targets from the same lab, with newer models, so it replaces the CodaLab runs here.

Scripts: `scripts/opinionqa_ladder.py`, `scripts/argyle_ladder.py`, `scripts/argyle_receipt_table15.py`. Results: `results/opinionqa/`, `results/argyle/`. Both scripts rerun in under a minute.

## Receipts

- **OpinionQA loading.** Our total variation for 26 model-method-group configurations reproduces the TV in Meister's own `eval_disagreement_bootstrapping.csv` to within 0.0006 on 24 of them. The two Llama-3-70B sequence rows differ by 0.005 and 0.018; their evaluation special-cases some sequence parsing (`results/opinionqa/receipt_tv_reproduction.csv`).
- **OpinionQA human targets.** For party, sex and race the script asserts that every stored target proportion equals the released Pew count divided by n, and that the target stored beside every model output equals the one in the unsteered file. All assertions pass.
- **Option letters.** Meister's prompt assigns letters A, B, C to the options in the order of each group's own count keys, which are alphabetical and drop options with zero count. Letters therefore mean different options for different groups on some questions. We map letters back to option names per group before any comparison (`mapping_audit.csv` lists the 90 group-question cells where the mapping could not be confirmed; they are excluded).
- **Argyle coding.** Our cleaning reproduces Argyle's complete-case subset exactly (N = 1,781) and all 15 means we checked from their Appendix Table 15 (`results/argyle/receipt_table15.csv`).

## How the rungs were translated

- **Level 2.** Same verdict rule as the paper, copied from `scripts/66_level2_permodel_equivalence.py`, with the bound set at the population gap. On OpinionQA the scalar is the expected ordinal position of the answer distribution, using OpinionQA's own `option_ordinal` field and rescaled to 0 to 1 per question (two nominal questions dropped, 98 left). A contrast's gap is averaged over questions, with each question oriented so the Pew gap is positive, and questions serve as the pairing unit in place of the paper's matched cells. On Argyle the gap is the difference in group means on the same respondents, with inference by respondent bootstrap (2,000 draws). Benjamini-Hochberg q within each model-method-steering family (OpinionQA) or each outcome (Argyle).
- **Level 3.** Strict tolerance: the human group mean's own 95% sampling half-width. Use tolerance: on OpinionQA, the model's plurality answer matches the Pew plurality answer, with a group passing when 90% of questions match (the criterion the paper's score-scale rule uses). On Argyle, 5 percentage points for proportions and one response category for ordinal scales. **These use tolerances are my placeholders**; the paper's rule is that the deployer states them.

## Result 1. OpinionQA (Meister 2024)

**Level 2.** 154 model-method-steering-contrast rows. Across all of them the models reproduce a median 0.56 of the Pew gap. The party gap survives best (median 0.94 of Pew's), sex next (0.78), and the racial, education and income gaps worst (0.30 to 0.54).

| Contrast | Pew gap (0-1 scale) | Median share of it reproduced | Kept | Missing | Steepened |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Republican - Democrat | 0.19 | 0.94 | 10/26 | 10/26 | 6/26 |
| Female - Male | 0.06 | 0.78 | 18/26 | 5/26 | 0 |
| Black - White | 0.10 | 0.46 | 5/26 | 21/26 | 0 |
| Hispanic - White | 0.08 | 0.46 | 5/20 | 15/20 | 0 |
| Asian - White | 0.09 | 0.54 | 4/20 | 16/20 | 0 |
| Less than HS - College+ | 0.08 | 0.47 | 3/12 | 7/12 | 0 |
| Income <$30k - $100k+ | 0.06 | 0.30 | 3/12 | 7/12 | 0 |
| South - Northeast | 0.03 | 0.78 | 3/12 | 4/12 | 2/12 |

Per model the median share runs from 0.20 (GPT-3.5) to 0.85 (Llama-3-70B, three contrasts only). GPT-3.5 under token log-probabilities reverses the income gap (ratio -0.94, 65% of questions pointing the wrong way). The pattern matches the paper's PHQ-8 result: racial gaps are the ones that go missing. Restricting to questions where the Pew gap is itself separable from zero changes little (missing 68, kept 44, steepened 4, undetermined 2; `level2_contrasts_sensitivity_separable_questions.csv`).

**Level 3.** No model-method-group cell passes either tolerance. A fresh Pew sample of the same size would match the plurality answer on 94% of questions; the models match it on 26% to 80% (median 57%). The strict tolerance would hold for 95% of questions in a fresh sample; the models hold it on 1% to 52%. Mean absolute error is 0.07 to 0.27 of the scale range (`level3_groups.csv`).

**Stops.** The gate needs repeat generations of one configuration, and each configuration was generated once. Level 1 needs individual respondents, and the release holds group distributions. Level 4 needs item-level responses within respondents. All three are recorded as stops.

Parse failures are low except Claude 3 Opus with verbalised distributions under persona steering (220 of 1,282 group-question cells, 17%), so that row rests on 51 to 70 questions per contrast (`parse_failures.csv`).

## Result 2. Argyle et al. 2023, Study 3

**Level 2.** 61 contrasts over 9 outcomes and 7 group axes; the 50 whose human gap is separable from zero are read. GPT-3 reproduces a median 0.54 of the human gap, **on the same respondents, with the group attribute printed in the backstory.** The largest losses:

- Party ID, Black - White: -2.23 points human, -0.85 silicon (0.38 of it).
- Patriotism (1 to 7, 1 = the flag makes them feel extremely good), Black - White: +1.05 human, -0.09 silicon. Patriotism, Republican - Democrat: -0.96 human, +0.05 silicon.
- Ideology, HS or less - Graduate: +0.67 human, +0.01 silicon.
- Trump share among voters, Black - White: -0.50 human, -0.27 silicon.

Verdicts on the main run: missing 29, kept 13, steepened 4, undetermined 4 (`results/argyle/level2_contrasts.csv`). The verdict for a contrast matches across the three temperature runs 64% of the time (0.7 against 1.0) and 70% (0.7 against 0.001), the paper's point that the verdict belongs to the model and its settings together.

**Level 3.** The strict tolerance holds in 4 of 116 outcome-by-group cells, and the placeholder use tolerance in 57 of 116. On the whole sample GPT-3 places respondents 0.54 points more Republican on party ID, 0.52 points more patriotic and 0.40 points more politically interested than they reported. Trump's share among voters comes out at 0.26 against 0.46, because GPT-3 answers "someone else" for 52% of the voters in the complete-case subset, a figure Argyle's own Table 15 reports (0.5). On the two-party share it is 0.50 against 0.52 and passes the use tolerance. The level-3 verdict turns on which quantity the use needs, which is why the paper makes the deployer state it.

**Gate diagnostic, not the gate.** The same respondent's silicon answer is identical across the 0.7 and 1.0 runs 29% of the time on party ID, 26% on ideology and 55% on church attendance (`gate_diagnostic_temperature_runs.csv`). Different temperatures bound regeneration instability from above; the gate itself needs repeats at one setting, which were not released.

**Stops.** Level 1: each silicon answer was generated separately from the human's other answers, so no silicon respondent exists whose answers could be checked against each other. Level 4 is feasible (Argyle's own Study 3 compares pooled association structure; the ladder's version compares it between groups) and was not run tonight.

## What the external runs found in the ladder itself

1. **The level-2 rule cannot return "flattened" when the gap is estimated precisely.** With the equivalence bound set at the full population gap, any simulated gap whose 90% interval sits between zero and the population value tests as equivalent to zero, and "missing" is checked first. On OpinionQA "missing" covers ratios from -0.45 to 0.82 and "flattened" occurs 0 times in 154 rows. On Argyle "missing" covers -0.49 to 0.92; the Republican - Democrat two-party vote gap reproduced at 0.92 of the human value is labelled missing. At half the bound, 64 of the 85 OpinionQA "missing" rows become "flattened" (`verdict_half_bound` column in both level-2 files). The caption of the paper's per-model level-2 table (tab:level2model) already says flattened "none occurs". **This needs fixing before BRM.** One option is to test equivalence to zero at half the population gap; another is to put the flattened test ahead of the missing test. The paper's racial verdicts would need rerunning under whichever rule you choose. The supplement already reports that neither racial gap is equivalent to zero at half the disparity.
2. **Level 2 needs a population gap that exists.** Where the human gap is near zero the bound collapses and ratios explode (political interest, Republican - Democrat: human -0.004, ratio 22). The paper ran only anchored contrasts with real gaps. The rule should state the precondition that the population gap be separable from zero.
3. **The stops are informative.** Neither public release supports the gate, and neither supports level 1. Both were designed for group-level comparison. That supports the paper's claim that no current protocol records where the reference runs out, and gives the tutorial a concrete "what to release" list.

## Caveats

- Pew counts in the Meister release are unweighted, and the ANES file carries no weights. Both comparisons are to the unweighted sample, which for Argyle is the right reference (same respondents).
- Orienting each OpinionQA question by the sign of the Pew gap inflates the human gap slightly on questions where it is near zero; the separable-questions sensitivity addresses it.
- Education, income and region targets in the Meister release come without counts, so those groups have no strict-tolerance test and their option-letter mapping is inferred (and dropped where it cannot be).
- The Argyle generation listing for Study 3 shows `temperature=0.001` inside the loop while their README calls the main file the 0.7 run. I followed the README.
